newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK inflation jumps to two-year high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK inflation jumps to two-year high.

text.p: Headline British inflation leapt to 3.3 percent in the year to July, its highest rate in nearly two years, from 2.9 percent in June, official figures showed on Tuesday.

The Office for National Statistics said underlying retail price inflation, excluding volatile home loan payments, also jumped -- to 3.0 percent year-on-year from 2.7 percent in June, well above the government's 2.5 percent target.
Headline RPI was last higher in September 1995, when it was rattling along at 3.9 percent.
The financial markets were unfazed, however. The FTSE-100 index of leading shares rose 11 points to 5,043. The pound was up a touch at around 2.95 marks.

Economists said the climb in July inflation was largely due to one-off effects, notably a jump in petrol prices following budget duty increases and increased housing costs after a series of recent interest rate rises.
"One factor that may prevent the markets selling off too badly on this is that RPIY fell on the month," said Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale .

RPIY cuts mortgage payments and indirect taxes out of the inflation equation, thus excluding any measures introduced in the July 2 budget. It fell 0.2 percent between June and July and was just 2.2 percent higher than a year ago.
Petrol and oil prices rocketed by 14 percent in the year to July after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown increased duty by four pence per litre in his first budget.

Mortgage rates, meanwhile, rose by an average 0.28 percentage points last month after the Bank of England's monetary policy committee, now free to move base rates, ratcheted them up by a quarter-point.

The Bank raised rates again last week in its ongoing quest to meet the government's inflation target two years out. That was the fourth quarter-point rise in as many months, taking base rates to seven percent.
Fears sparked by the headline figures were also tempered by a 1.5 percent drop in household goods prices over the month and a 4.7 percent slide in clothes and footwear prices.

The Bank is worried that a flood of windfall payments from building societies converting into banks -- 35 billion pounds in free shares at the last count -- will push already-buoyant high street spending into an inflationary boom. But maybe it should relax.

Sales data show consumers have spent their windfalls on goods like washing machines and televisions, which come under the heading of household goods. But retailers have failed to crank up prices in response.

"There are still no signs of any meaningful upward pressure on prices," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "The implication is consumers are still being very fussy about prices, even when spending their windfalls."

Nonetheless, all eyes will be on the Bank's quarterly inflation report, to be released on Wednesday. Last week it hinted that its latest rate rise may be the last for some time, saying base rates were now at a level consistent with keeping inflation on target in two years' time.

"I think... the rate rises we have had already, along with the fiscal tightening from the budget, will be enough to get inflation under control and on target next year," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.
The Bank has to balance the demands of a two-speed economy -- booming retail and service sectors versus a manufacturing base battered by a meteoric rise in the pound.

But here too, Tuesday's figures offered some comfort. Inflation in the service sector, where most economists perceive the greatest threat to lurk, dropped to 2.9 percent year-on-year, from 3.2 in June. "This adds support to our view that fears of a take-off in service-sector inflation this year have been well overdone," Loynes said.
